abstract: Dr. Calvert reviews vulvar anatomy and normal variants, then teaches systematic lesion description using location, color, texture, and morphology. The lecture covers common benign findings (ectopic sebaceous glands, epidermal inclusion cysts, angiokeratomas, lentigo) and distinguishes them from concerning lesions like melanoma and HPV warts. Lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are discussed in detail, emphasizing diagnostic features (silver sheen, atrophy, fusion, oral involvement) and management differences. The session stresses the importance of palpation to assess firmness and the need for biopsy of suspicious pigmented or firm lesions.
key_points: Use anatomic landmarks (mons, clitoral hood, urethra, labia majora/minora, fourchette, perineum) and clock-face orientation to precisely document vulvar lesions.
Normal labia minora vary widely in size, symmetry, and pigmentation; symmetric variants are normal and require only reassurance.
Palpation is essential: HPV warts are hard and firm, while normal papillae and skin tags are soft; firmness raises concern for malignancy.
Ectopic sebaceous glands appear as small, raised, yellow-white spots on labia minora; they are benign and cannot be removed without excision.
Epidermal inclusion cysts are firm, filled with exfoliated skin, and cannot be drained; definitive treatment requires excision of the cyst wall.
Angiokeratomas are common, benign, black-to-red pinpoint papules often clustered on labia majora (or scrotum in males); reassurance is the main management.
Lichen sclerosus presents with pale, atrophic, thin skin with a silver sheen, often with labial fusion; it causes intense itching and requires high-potency topical steroids.
Lichen sclerosus increases skin cancer risk; patients need vulvar exams every six months to monitor for firm, raised lesions that may burrow deep.
Lichen planus features tender, eroded areas without significant lichenification; look for oral lacy white plaques (Wickham striae) to aid diagnosis.
Herpes simplex shows grouped vesicles in various stages (clear, purulent, scabbed) simultaneously; folliculitis is centered on hair follicles and not grouped.
Melanoma warning signs: irregular borders, multiple colors (black, blue, red, white), raised areas; any suspicious pigmented lesion warrants biopsy and referral.
Postmenopausal atrophy can cause itching, but lichen sclerosus is distinguished by silver sheen, fusion, and lack of response to standard itch treatments.
